title: A comparison with another grammar guide (part 2): the copula
summary: The second commentary looks at how the copula だ and です are treated, and why the course keeps them as one logical element.

blocks.text: This is the second commentary episode. Last time the subject was が; this time it is the copula. The course argues that a model which makes だ a vague declarative marker takes away one of the pillars of Japanese structure.
The teaching of the copula is in lesson 79. This note only looks at how it is treated in the other guide.

A logical Japanese sentence can end in only three ways: with a **verb**, with an **adjective**, or with a **noun plus the copula**. A bare noun is not an engine. The course's strongest evidence that だ is a real engine is that it changes form, just like verbs and adjectives.

rows: a person who is a student

blocks.text: In casual speech だ and particles are often dropped. That does not mean they are unnecessary.
English does the same: "Got up early this morning" drops the "I", yet everyone understands it. Dropping is a legal shortcut because the listener can fill the gap.

blocks.en: Sakura, Japanese. (casual, だ and は dropped)

blocks.text: Dropped but understood: the listener fills the gap.

items: Three ways to end a logical sentence: verb, adjective, noun + copula.
だ changes form like a verb or adjective: だった, で, な, だろう.
In casual speech だ can be dropped, but it is still understood.
